# Objectives

In this example we will:

- Explore two spatially correlated variables: the concentrations of **lead** (primary variable) and **zinc** (secondary variable) in the Meuse soil samples.
- Compute the **direct semivariograms** of both variables and their **cross-semivariogram**.
- Fit a **linear model of coregionalization**, the joint model required by co-kriging.

::: {.callout-tip title="R script"}
You can download the R script with all the code of this example and follow it step by step in RStudio:

{{< downloadthis scripts/Chapter3_Example1.R dname="Chapter3_Example1" label="Download the R script" icon="file-earmark-code" type="outline-success" >}}
:::

# Packages

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(gstat)
library(sf)
```

# Description of the data

::: {.callout-note title="Why lead?"}
Lead (Pb) is a serious human health hazard: it can be inhaled as dust from disturbed
soil, or taken up by plants and ingested. As a reference, the Berlin Digital
Environmental Atlas establishes the following guide values for lead in soils:

- above 600 mg/kg, grain crops cannot be grown for human consumption;
- above 300 mg/kg, crops must be tested;
- above 100 mg/kg, consumption of leafy vegetables should be avoided;
- below 200 mg/kg is required for sports fields or parks.

Natural levels in unpolluted soils are around 30 mg/kg. In the Meuse data, lead
ranges from 37 to 654 mg/kg, and more than half of the samples exceed 100 mg/kg.
:::

The `meuse` dataset (included in the `sp` package) contains 155 soil samples collected in the floodplain of the river Meuse (the Netherlands), with the concentrations of several heavy metals (in ppm, i.e., mg/kg). The coordinates are expressed in the Dutch national grid (EPSG:28992), in metres.

```{r}
data(meuse, package="sp")        # soil samples
data(meuse.riv, package="sp")    # outline of the river

meuse_sf <- meuse |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  st_as_sf(coords=c("x","y"), crs=28992)

river <- list(meuse.riv) |>
  st_polygon() |>
  st_sfc(crs = 28992)

head(meuse_sf)
head(river)
```
Both metals come from the same industrial sources and are transported in the same way by the river floods, so we expect them to show a similar spatial pattern:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
#| fig-cap: Lead and zinc concentrations (ppm) in the Meuse soil samples, classified by quintiles.
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 9

pal <- hcl.colors(5, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE)

draw_map <- function(var, title) {
  br <- quantile(meuse_sf[[var]], probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2))
  cl <- cut(meuse_sf[[var]], br, include.lowest = TRUE)
  bb <- st_bbox(meuse_sf)
  plot(st_geometry(river), col = "lightblue", border = NA,
       xlim = bb[c(1, 3)], ylim = bb[c(2, 4)], main = title)
  plot(st_geometry(meuse_sf), pch = 21, bg = pal[cl], col = "grey30",
       cex = 1.1, add = TRUE)
  box()
  legend("topleft", legend = paste(round(br[-6]), "-", round(br[-1])),
         pt.bg = pal, pch = 21, col = "grey30", title = "ppm",
         bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
draw_map("lead", "Lead (Pb)")
draw_map("zinc", "Zinc (Zn)")
```

Both maps show the same pattern: higher concentrations near the river and lower concentrations further away from it.

## Log transformation of lead and zinc variables  {.unnumbered}

Heavy metal concentrations usually have very **right-skewed** distributions: many low values and a few very high ones.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
hist(meuse_sf$lead, main = "Lead", xlab = "ppm", col = "grey80")
hist(meuse_sf$zinc, main = "Zinc", xlab = "ppm", col = "grey80")
hist(log(meuse_sf$lead), main = "log(Lead)", xlab = "log(ppm)", col = "grey80")
hist(log(meuse_sf$zinc), main = "log(Zinc)", xlab = "log(ppm)", col = "grey80")
```

We will work with both variables on the **log scale** because:

- The log transformation makes their distributions approximately symmetric.
- The empirical semivariogram is based on squared differences, so it is very sensitive to extreme values. The log transformation stabilizes it.
- Co-kriging is based on linear relationships between the variables, and on the log scale the relationship between lead and zinc is slightly more linear.
- Both variables are on the same scale, which makes the sills of the cross-semivariogram easier to interpret.

::: {.callout-note}
Predictions obtained on the log scale must be back-transformed with `exp()`. This back-transformation approximately gives the **median**, not the mean, on the original scale.
:::

# Semivariogram of the primary variable

Before working with both variables, we analyse the primary variable (lead) on its own, as in Chapter 1.

## Empirical semivariogram

```{r}
v_lead <- variogram(log(lead) ~ 1, meuse_sf)
v_lead
```

- The term `~ 1` in the formula means a **constant mean** (no trend).
- By default, the maximum distance (`cutoff`) is one third of the diagonal of the bounding box of the data, divided into 15 distance lags (`width = cutoff/15`).

*Remember*: each row of the output corresponds to a distance lag

| Column | Meaning | Notation |
|---|---|---|
| `np` | Number of pairs of observations in the lag | $\lvert N(h)\rvert$ |
| `dist` | Mean distance of these pairs (m) | $h$ |
| `gamma` | Empirical semivariance | $\hat\gamma(h)$ |

::: {.callout-note title="Interpretation"}
For example, the first row indicates that there are `r v_lead$np[1]` pairs of samples separated by a mean distance of `r round(v_lead$dist[1])` m, with an empirical semivariance of `r round(v_lead$gamma[1], 3)`.
:::


## Fitted theoretical model

```{r}
vgm_lead <- fit.variogram(v_lead, model=vgm(psill=0.5, model="Sph",
                                            range=1000, nugget=0.05))
vgm_lead
```

The function `vgm()` defines a theoretical model with **initial values** for its parameters (chosen by visual inspection):

| Argument | Meaning | Notation |
|---|---|---|
| `model = "Sph"` | Spherical model | — |
| `psill = 0.5` | Partial sill | $\sigma^2$ |
| `range = 1000` | Range (for the spherical model, the exact range) | $\rho$ |
| `nugget = 0.05` | Nugget effect | $\tau^2$ |

The function `fit.variogram()` then fits the model to the empirical semivariogram by **weighted least squares** (Chapter 2).

::: {.callout-note title="Interpretation of the fitted model"}
- Nugget effect: $\tau^2 \approx$ `r round(vgm_lead$psill[1], 3)`.
- Partial sill: $\sigma^2 \approx$ `r round(vgm_lead$psill[2], 3)`.
- Total sill: $\tau^2+\sigma^2 \approx$ `r round(sum(vgm_lead$psill), 3)`. The nugget effect represents about `r round(100 * vgm_lead$psill[1] / sum(vgm_lead$psill))`% of the total sill: the variability at very short distances is small.
- Range: $\rho \approx$ `r round(vgm_lead$range[2])` m. Beyond this distance, lead concentrations in two samples are no longer correlated. 
:::

```{r}
#| fig-show: hide
plot(v_lead, vgm_lead, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     main = "Semivariogram of log-lead (Pb)")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
library(lattice)

# Parameters of the fitted model
nugget <- vgm_lead$psill[1]          # nugget effect
sill   <- sum(vgm_lead$psill)        # total sill
rng    <- vgm_lead$range[2]          # range

plot(v_lead, vgm_lead, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     main = "Semivariogram of log-lead (Pb)",
     xlim = c(0, 1600), ylim = c(0, 0.7),
     panel = function(...) {
       vgm.panel.xyplot(...)   # empirical points + fitted model
       # total sill and range
       panel.abline(h = sill, lty = 2, col = "red")
       panel.abline(v = rng,  lty = 2, col = "blue")
       # nugget and partial sill
       panel.arrows(60, 0, 60, nugget, length = 0.06, code = 3,
                    col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
       panel.arrows(1300, nugget, 1300, sill, length = 0.06, code = 3,
                    col = "orange", lwd = 2)
       # labels
       panel.text(60, nugget / 2, "nugget", pos = 4, col = "darkgreen")
       panel.text(1300, (nugget + sill) / 2, "partial sill", pos = 4, col = "orange")
       panel.text(20, sill, "total sill", adj = c(0, -0.5), col = "red")
       panel.text(rng, 0.05, "range", pos = 4, col = "blue")
     })
```

# Direct and cross-empirical semivariograms

To work with both variables jointly, we create a `gstat` object containing them:

```{r}
g <- gstat(NULL, id = "Pb", formula = log(lead) ~ 1, data = meuse_sf)
g <- gstat(g,    id = "Zn", formula = log(zinc) ~ 1, data = meuse_sf)
g
```

When `variogram()` is applied to an object with two variables, `gstat` computes the **three empirical semivariograms** at once:

```{r}
v <- variogram(g)
```

| `id` | Semivariogram | Notation |
|---|---|---|
| `Pb` | Direct semivariogram of lead | $\hat\gamma_{11}(h)$ |
| `Zn` | Direct semivariogram of zinc | $\hat\gamma_{22}(h)$ |
| `Pb.Zn` | Cross-semivariogram | $\hat\gamma_{12}(h)$ |

For the cross-semivariogram, the product of the differences of both variables is used for each pair of locations, instead of the squared difference of a single variable. Therefore, it can only be computed at the locations where both variables have been measured (in the Meuse data, all of them).

::: {.callout-tip}
- The direct semivariogram of lead (`id = "Pb"`) is exactly the same as `v_lead`, computed in the previous section.
- In the cross-semivariogram, the number of pairs `np` is twice that of the direct semivariograms, because `gstat` counts each pair of locations in both possible orders. This does not affect the value of the semivariance.
:::

```{r}
v |> 
  filter(id=="Pb") |> 
  select(np, dist, gamma) |> 
  head()

v |> 
  filter(id=="Pb.Zn") |> 
  select(np, dist, gamma) |> 
  head()
```

# Linear model of coregionalization

The three semivariograms cannot be fitted separately: the joint model must be valid. In the **linear model of coregionalization**, the three semivariograms share the same basic structures (same shape and same range) and differ only in their sills.

```{r}
lmc <- fit.lmc(v, g, model=vgm_lead)
lmc$model
```

The function `fit.lmc()` takes:

- the empirical semivariograms (`v`);
- the `gstat` object with both variables (`g`);
- the model fitted for lead (`vgm_lead`), from which it takes the **basic structures** (nugget effect + spherical model) and the **range** (`r round(vgm_lead$range[2])` m).

It keeps the range fixed and fits only the **sills** of each semivariogram. The result is again a `gstat` object, now including the fitted models, which will be used for co-kriging predictions (`predict()`) and cross-validation (`gstat.cv()`).

::: {.callout-note}
The range is taken from the direct semivariogram of lead, which implicitly assumes that it is also adequate for zinc and for the cross-semivariogram. Looking at the plot below, this assumption is reasonable. Alternatively, `fit.lmc(..., fit.ranges = TRUE)` also refits the common range using the three semivariograms jointly.
:::

## Plot of the fitted model {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Direct and cross empirical semivariograms of log-lead (Pb) and log-zinc (Zn), with the fitted linear model of coregionalization."

plot(v, lmc, pch = 19, col = "black",
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     scales = list(alternating = 1, tck = c(1, 0)))
```

In each panel, the **points** are the empirical semivariograms (computed with `variogram()`) and the **lines** are the fitted linear model of coregionalization (`fit.lmc()`).

::: {.callout-note title="Interpretation"}
The cross-semivariogram shows a clear spatial structure, very similar to that of the direct semivariograms: it increases with distance and levels off at about `r round(sum(lmc$model$Pb.Zn$psill), 2)`. This indicates a **strong spatial correlation** between both metals, so zinc can provide useful information to predict lead in co-kriging.
:::

# Summary of the workflow

| Step | Function | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Empirical semivariogram of the primary variable | `variogram()` | Points |
| Theoretical model of the primary variable | `fit.variogram()` | Line (shape and range) |
| Direct and cross empirical semivariograms | `gstat()` + `variogram()` | Points of the three semivariograms |
| Linear model of coregionalization | `fit.lmc()` | Lines of the three semivariograms (same shape, different sills) |


# Exercise

Repeat the analysis using **organic matter** (`om`) as the secondary variable instead of zinc. Note that:

- `om` has missing values, which must be removed first (`meuse_sf |> filter(!is.na(om))`).
- As in the example, use both variables on the **log scale** (`log(lead)` and `log(om)`).

Answer the following questions:

- Is the cross-semivariogram between lead and organic matter structured?
- How does it compare with the cross-semivariogram between lead and zinc?

## Solution {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
#| purl: false
# 1. Data -----------------------------------------------------

# om has missing values: remove those samples first
meuse_om <- meuse_sf |>
  filter(!is.na(om))
print(meuse_om)

# Correlation between lead and organic matter (log scale) at the same sampling points
cor(log(meuse_om$lead), log(meuse_om$om))


# 2. Semivariogram of the primary variable --------------------
v_lead <- variogram(log(lead) ~ 1, meuse_om)
vgm_lead <- fit.variogram(v_lead,
                          model = vgm(psill = 0.5, model = "Sph",
                                      range = 1000, nugget = 0.05))
vgm_lead


# 3. Direct and cross empirical semivariograms -----------------
g <- gstat(NULL, id = "Pb", formula = log(lead) ~ 1, data = meuse_om)
g <- gstat(g,    id = "OM", formula = log(om) ~ 1,   data = meuse_om)

v <- variogram(g)


# 4. Linear model of coregionalization -------------------------
lmc <- fit.lmc(v, g, model = vgm_lead)
lmc$model
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# 5. Plot -----------------------------------------------------
plot(v, lmc, pch = 19, col = "black",
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     scales = list(alternating = 1, tck = c(1, 0)))
```
| | Example (Pb and Zn) | Exercise (Pb and OM) |
|---|---|---|
| Number of samples | 155 | 153 |
| Correlation at the same sampling points (log scale) | 0.97 | 0.53 |
| Common range | $\approx$ 965 m | $\approx$ 1028 m |
| Cross-semivariogram sill: nugget effect | 0.048 | 0.002 |
| Cross-semivariogram sill: spherical model | 0.544 | 0.227 |
| Total sill of the cross-semivariogram | $\approx$ 0.59 | $\approx$ 0.23 |

: Comparison of the linear models of coregionalization for lead and zinc (example) and lead and organic matter (exercise). {#tbl-comparison}


**Interpretation:**

- The cross-semivariogram between lead and organic matter **is structured**: it increases with distance and levels off, so there is a spatial correlation between both variables.
- However, this correlation is **considerably weaker** than with zinc (@tbl-comparison): the sill of the cross-semivariogram is much lower ($0.23$ vs. $0.59$), and the correlation at the same sampling points is also lower ($0.53$ vs. $0.97$). For the nugget effect component, the cross-semivariogram sill is almost zero: at very short distances, the variations of both variables are practically independent.
- **Conclusion for co-kriging:** zinc is a much better secondary variable to predict lead. Organic matter could provide some information, but less.
